newsitem.title: FRANCE: New French probe opens into seized Jewish property.
newsitem.headline: New French probe opens into seized Jewish property.

text.p: A French bank has opened a probe into the fate of millions of francs (dollars) in cash, jewelry and other valuables entrusted to it after being seized from Jews headed for Nazi gas chambers during World War Two.

Pierre Saragoussi of the state-owned Caisse des Depots et Consignations on Monday estimated the current value of the seized cash plus the proceeds from the sale of the valuables at 24 million francs ($4.3 million).
But the bank did not know in which accounts the money had been deposited, he told reporters.
After the war, the Caisse returned to owners or heirs the equivalent of about 1.3 billion francs ($236 million) seized from bank accounts or resulting from forced sales.
The sum now at stake is much smaller but its origins are more poignant since it involves such valuables as wedding bands and watches taken from people at the time they were arrested.
The probe follows the government's decision last week to appoint a commission to investigate what happened to Jewish property taken during the wartime Nazi occupation.
Most attention has fallen on the mystery surrounding nearly 2,000 art works, including paintings by Gauguin, Renoir and Rodin, "provisionally" administered by French museums for more than 50 years.
The commission is to try to determine whether the works belonged to Jews who disappeared in Nazi death camps.

But the sums now involved generally came not from rich art collectors but from poor Eastern European immigrants who made up most of the 67,000 Jews who passed through Drancy camp near Paris on the way to gas chambers at Auschwitz in Poland.
Altogether, some 76,000 of the 320,000 Jews then in France were sent to Nazi concentration camps, including 11,000 children. Only about 2,800 of those deported survived.
Saragoussi speculated the sums seized at Drancy and handed to his bank for safekeeping by the collaborationist Vichy regime went to accounts administered by the Paris police.
"Either an account was frozen in 1945 or it was activated some time after," Saragoussi said, explaining that the bank would seek to determine where the funds went.
Sighs of relief were heard at the Paris town hall where an expert commission reported that only eight of 350 city-owned flats or buildings now on sale might be seized Jewish property.
A recent book had said that city authorities might be administering hundreds of flats that had been left vacant by Jews killed in concentration camps.

Deputy mayor Lucien Finel, who narrowly escaped arrest and whose own family disappeared in Nazi camps, said he was not surprised by the findings since most death camp victims were poor people who rented rather than owned their flats.

Efforts are also under way in several other countries to shed light on the dark years of World War Two including neutral Switzerland and Sweden, accused of profitably dealing with the Nazis and being paid in gold seized from Jews.

French Jewish leaders have been at pains to stress that their community, which now numbers 750,000 and is Western Europe's largest, sought to bring out the truth about the past but did not want financial compensation.
